summaries.example: Suppose you hear thunder and then see dark clouds. These clues may give you a reason to believe that rain is coming. But if a weather expert says the sound was part of a movie, that new information may weaken your reason. Evidence can help, but it can sometimes mislead us.
summaries.summary: Evidence is what helps us decide what to believe. Philosophers ask what evidence really is. It might be a physical object, a fact, something we know, an experience, or a mental state. Different ideas emphasize different jobs for evidence. Evidence can justify a belief, guide us toward truth, and help people compare ideas. Still, evidence does not guarantee that a belief is true. A clue can be misleading, and new evidence can weaken an old reason. Philosophers also ask whether evidence must be public and shareable or whether private experiences can count. These questions show why the everyday word “evidence” has a deeper philosophical puzzle behind it.
key_ideas: Evidence helps us decide what is reasonable to believe.
A person should consider all the relevant evidence, not just one favorite clue.
Evidence can point toward truth, but it can also be misleading.
Some evidence can be shared publicly, while other evidence may be personal, such as a headache.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use evidence when solving mysteries, checking news, doing science, and making everyday choices. Thinking carefully about evidence helps us avoid believing something just because we want it to be true. It also reminds us to listen for new information and to distinguish being wrong from being unreasonable. A careful thinker follows the evidence available, while remembering that even good evidence may not give complete certainty.

important_terms.definition: Information, objects, or experiences that give us a reason to believe something.
A good reason for holding a belief, even though the belief might still be wrong.
A clue that points toward something else, such as smoke pointing toward fire.
New information that weakens or defeats an earlier reason for belief.

questions_to_think_about: Can a clue be useful evidence even when it leads to a wrong belief?
What new information could change your mind about something?
Is evidence always something that other people can see too?

summaries.example: A meteorologist studies weather data and predicts rain. The data are first-order evidence for the prediction. If another person learns that the meteorologist is usually reliable, that fact can function as higher-order evidence: it is evidence about how the original evidence was assessed. But using both the data and the expert’s conclusion may risk counting the same information twice. The example shows that evidence can concern the world, or the reliability and interpretation of other evidence.
summaries.summary: The philosophical problem of evidence is difficult partly because evidence is expected to perform several jobs. In epistemology, evidence is commonly treated as what justifies belief: it changes what a thinker is reasonable in believing. Evidentialist views make justification depend on total evidence, while Bayesian approaches also allow prior probabilities to affect rational belief. Evidence is defeasible, so later information may undercut the link between a reason and a conclusion or rebut the conclusion by supporting its opposite. Rational response to evidence is not the same as truth; misleading experiences can produce false but nonculpable beliefs. A different approach treats evidence as a sign or reliable indicator of truth. Yet an indicator may fail to justify someone who does not know the relevant connection, so philosophers distinguish indicator evidence from normative evidence. Scientific inquiry also raises questions about evidence as a public, objective arbiter. Evidence can promote agreement, but background theories, priors, paradigms, and possible theory-ladenness may affect how it is understood. The entry therefore presents evidence as a concept shaped by competing demands: justification, truth, rational responsiveness, and intersubjective objectivity.
key_ideas: Evidence is closely connected with justification: it affects what it is reasonable to believe.
The relevant standard is usually a person’s total evidence, because additional information can defeat an initially good reason.
Rationality does not guarantee truth. A person may respond responsibly to evidence that happens to be misleading.
Evidence may be understood as a reliable sign in the world, but that is not automatically the same as evidence that a person can use to justify belief.
The force of evidence can depend on background knowledge, prior probabilities, or other features of inquiry.
Evidence is often expected to be public and capable of producing agreement, yet private experiences may also seem to justify beliefs.
summaries.why_it_matters: Beliefs guide inquiry, decisions, science, law, and everyday judgment. Understanding evidence helps explain why a belief can be reasonable without being true, why new information can change a conclusion, and why disagreement may persist even among informed thinkers. It also clarifies a central tension in philosophy of science: evidence should be objective and shareable enough to assess competing theories, but some justified beliefs seem grounded in personal experience. Examining these tensions encourages careful reasoning without pretending that every dispute has a simple resolution.

important_terms.definition: The view that what a person is justified in believing is determined by that person’s total evidence.
Evidence that supports a belief only until additional information undermines or outweighs it.
Evidence that weakens the connection between an initial reason and its conclusion.
Evidence that supports the opposite of the conclusion supported by an initial reason.
Evidence that directly bears on a hypothesis or claim.
Evidence about the force, reliability, or interpretation of first-order evidence.
The idea that evidence is a reliable indicator or mark of what it concerns.
Evidence understood as what tends to make a belief reasonable for a particular thinker.

questions_to_think_about: If two people share the same data but have different background assumptions, must they reach the same conclusion?
When does an expert’s judgment count as evidence, and when might relying on it duplicate the original evidence?
Can someone be fully rational while holding a false belief because the available evidence is misleading?
Should evidence be limited to what a person knows, or can experiences and mental states also count?
Does the theory-ladenness of observation limit evidence’s ability to settle disputes?

summaries.example: Your classmate says the school team won because they heard an announcement. At first, that testimony is evidence for the claim. Later, you learn that the announcement came from a student known for making up stories. This is an undercutting defeater: it weakens the connection between the testimony and the claim. If a coach then says the team lost, that is a rebutting defeater because it supports the opposite result.
summaries.summary: Philosophers study evidence because it affects what people are justified in believing and how inquiry can aim at truth. One influential approach, evidentialism, says that justification depends on a person’s evidence, especially the total evidence available rather than a single supporting fact. Evidence is often defeasible: a new fact may weaken an earlier reason or support the opposite conclusion. Rational thinkers should adjust their beliefs to the strength of the evidence, although careful reasoning can still lead to a false belief when the evidence is misleading. Another approach understands evidence as a sign or reliable indicator, such as smoke indicating fire. But a reliable connection in the world does not automatically help someone who does not know that connection. Scientific evidence is also expected to be public and objective, so that different investigators can compare results. The source notes that background theories, prior assumptions, and disagreements about observation can complicate this ideal.
key_ideas: Evidence is tied to justification, or what a person has reason to believe.
Good reasoning requires responding to the whole body of evidence, including information that weakens earlier reasons.
Being rational means responding appropriately to available evidence, not always arriving at the truth.
Evidence may be a clue that reliably points to a fact, but a clue is not always usable justification without background knowledge.
Shared evidence can support objectivity, yet people with different theories or starting assumptions may interpret the same evidence differently.
summaries.why_it_matters: Evidence affects how we judge rumors, arguments, reports, and scientific claims. Learning how evidence can be defeated helps us avoid clinging to a conclusion after important new information appears. The topic also teaches intellectual humility: a person can reason responsibly and still be mistaken. At the same time, asking whether evidence is private or public, and whether theories shape observation, helps explain why some disagreements are difficult even when people are trying to think carefully.

important_terms.definition: A reason or information that makes a belief more reasonable to hold.
The condition of having enough reason to believe something, even when it may turn out to be false.
The complete set of relevant information a thinker has, rather than one isolated clue.
Information that makes an earlier piece of evidence less useful or convincing.
A defeater that attacks the link between a reason and the belief it originally supported.
A defeater that supports the opposite of the belief originally supported.
A clue or pattern that reliably points toward something else.
The idea that evidence can be shared and assessed by more than one person.

questions_to_think_about: Why is a trustworthy witness’s statement stronger evidence than an unknown person’s statement?
Can evidence support a claim for one person but not for another who lacks important background knowledge?
Should a private feeling or pain count as evidence if nobody else can directly experience it?
Does disagreement prove that one side ignored the evidence?
How can new evidence restore confidence in an old belief that was previously defeated?
